before.claim: The vector $e_1=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ belongs to $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ because its entries sum to $1$ and its $\ell^1$ norm is $1\le C$. Thus the coefficient set is nonempty. It is closed: the sum constraint is the inverse image of the closed singleton $\{1\}$ under a continuous linear map, and the $\ell^1$ bound is the inverse image of the closed interval $(-\infty,C]$ under the continuous function $c\mapsto\sum_i|c_i|$. It is bounded because $\|c\|_1^2=\sum_i c_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}|c_i||c_j|\ge\|c\|_2^2$ and $\|c\|_1\le C$. Therefore [F2] makes $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ compact.

The map $c\mapsto\sum_i c_iR_i$ is linear and continuous in finite dimensions, and its squared Frobenius norm is continuous by [F1]. The extreme-value theorem gives a minimum; its minimizer set is closed as the inverse image of the singleton containing that minimum, hence compact as a closed subset of $\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Thus [F2] gives a nonempty compact set $M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\mathcal C_{s,C}}J(c)$.

The set $M$ is convex: $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ is convex, and for matrices $A,B$ the identity $\|(1-t)A+tB\|_F^2=(1-t)\|A\|_F^2+t\|B\|_F^2-t(1-t)\|A-B\|_F^2$ proves convexity of the squared norm. Applying it to $A=\sum_i c_iR_i$ and $B=\sum_i d_iR_i$ shows $J((1-t)c+td)\le(1-t)J(c)+tJ(d)=\min J$, so the convex combination also minimizes. Since $M$ is compact, the continuous function $c\mapsto\|c\|_2^2$ has a minimizer $c_*\in M$.

If distinct $c,d\in M$ both had minimum Euclidean norm, their midpoint would lie in $M$ and satisfy $\left\|\frac{c+d}{2}\right\|_2^2=\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2}-\frac{\|c-d\|_2^2}{4}<\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2},$ contradicting minimality. Thus $c_*$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares minimizer. No nonsingularity of the Gram matrix is needed for existence or tie-breaking.

before.quote:
Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

before.claim: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ of $F(X)$ with the eigenvalues in the given order. The strict gap prevents an eigenspace for one eigenvalue from straddling positions $r$ and $r+1$, so the sum of the first $r$ eigenspaces is the span of exactly the first $r$ basis vectors.

Changing the orthonormal basis within a repeated eigenspace below the gap leaves that entire eigenspace in the sum; changing one within a repeated eigenspace above the gap leaves that entire eigenspace out. Thus the selected subspace does not depend on the eigenbasis chosen in step 1.1. Its orthogonal projector is $P=\sum_{j=1}^r u_ju_j^*$, which satisfies $P=P^*$, $P^2=P$, and $\operatorname{tr}P=r$.

The operator in step 2.1 is independent of all allowed basis choices, lies in $\mathcal P_r$ by [L1], and is exactly the map specified by [F2]. Hence it is the unique rank-$r$ occupied spectral projector.

after.claim: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ of $F(X)$ with the eigenvalues in the given order. The strict gap prevents an eigenspace for one eigenvalue from straddling positions $r$ and $r+1$, so the sum of the first $r$ eigenspaces is the span of exactly the first $r$ basis vectors.

Changing the orthonormal basis within a repeated eigenspace below the gap leaves that entire eigenspace in the sum; changing one within a repeated eigenspace above the gap leaves that entire eigenspace out. Thus the selected subspace does not depend on the eigenbasis chosen in step 1.1. Its orthogonal projector is $P=\sum_{j=1}^r u_ju_j^*$, which satisfies $P=P^*$ and $P^2=P$ by orthonormality. By [F3], $\operatorname{tr}P=\sum_{a=1}^n P_{aa}=\sum_{a=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (u_j)_a\overline{(u_j)_a}=\sum_{j=1}^r\sum_{a=1}^n|(u_j)_a|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r1=r$, since each $u_j$ is a unit vector.

The operator in step 2.1 is independent of all allowed basis choices, lies in $\mathcal P_r$ by [L1], and is exactly the map specified by [F2]. Hence it is the unique rank-$r$ occupied spectral projector.

before.quote:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $n\ge2$, $1\le r<n$, and use the real Hermitian matrix space $\mathbb H_n$
and projector set $\mathcal P_r$ of
[[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]]. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb H_n$ be open
and let $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$ be a specified map. For a Hermitian matrix $H$,
write its eigenvalues with multiplicity in ascending order as
$$\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H).$$
Write $\sigma(H):=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$ for its finite spectrum,
with multiplicity omitted in this set notation.
For any Hermitian $H$ with $\lambda_r(H)<\lambda_{r+1}(H)$, write $\Pi_r(H)$
for the orthogonal projector onto the sum of eigenspaces belonging to its $r$
lowest eigenvalues. At a point $X\in U$ where
$$\lambda_r(F(X))<\lambda_{r+1}(F(X)),$$
define $\Phi(X):=\Pi_r(F(X))$. The strict gap separates the occupied cluster
from the unoccupied cluster; eigenvalue multiplicities within either cluster
are allowed. The construction's well-definedness as a unique member of
$\mathcal P_r$ is proved in [[lem-gapped-projector-map-well-defined]].

A set $K\subseteq U$ has a **uniform occupied/unoccupied gap** $g>0$ when the
displayed gap is at least $g$ for every $X\in K$. A self-consistent fixed point
is a point $X_*$ with $\Phi(X_*)=X_*$. Its fixed-point residual is
$\rho(X):=\|X-\Phi(X)\|_F$ whenever $\Phi(X)$ is defined. The map is not
asserted to be contractive merely because its gap is positive.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $r$ be an integer with $1\le r<n$. Use Hermitian
adjoints and matrices as in [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], trace as in
[[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]], and the Frobenius norm as in
[[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. Write
$$\mathbb H_n:=\{A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}:A=A^*\}$$
for the real vector space of Hermitian matrices, with Frobenius inner product
$$\langle A,B\rangle_F:=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)=\operatorname{tr}(AB).$$
The **rank-$r$ orthogonal projector domain** is
$$\mathcal P_r:=\{P\in\mathbb H_n:P^2=P,\ \operatorname{tr}P=r\}.$$
An element of $\mathcal P_r$ is an orthogonal projector; its range is the occupied
subspace. The statement that its range has dimension $r$ is justified by
[[lem-hermitian-idempotent-trace-equals-rank]]. A frame $Y\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}$
with $Y^*Y=I_r$ represents $P=YY^*$; replacing $Y$ by $YQ$ for a unitary
$Q\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}$ leaves $P$ unchanged.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

before.claim: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis for $P$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$. Idempotence gives $\lambda_j^2=\lambda_j$, so each $\lambda_j$ is $0$ or $1$.

In this basis the trace is $\sum_j\lambda_j$, while the image is spanned exactly by the eigenvectors with eigenvalue $1$. By [F2], the rank is the dimension of this image. Thus the trace and rank both equal the number of indices with $\lambda_j=1$.

after.claim: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis for $P$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$. Idempotence gives $\lambda_j^2=\lambda_j$, so each $\lambda_j$ is $0$ or $1$.

Let $U$ be the unitary matrix whose columns are the eigenbasis from step 1.1, so $U^*PU=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$. Since $U$ is unitary, $U^*=U^{-1}$ and [F3] gives $\operatorname{tr}P=\operatorname{tr}(U^*PU)=\sum_j\lambda_j$, where the last equality is the diagonal definition of trace. The image is spanned exactly by the eigenvectors with eigenvalue $1$, so by [F2] its dimension, and thus the rank, is the number of indices with $\lambda_j=1$. Therefore trace and rank agree.

before.quote:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map whose domain $V$ is finite-dimensional over
$F$. Its **nullity** and **rank** are

$$\operatorname{nullity}T:=\dim_F(\ker T),\qquad \operatorname{rank}T:=\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Both dimensions are defined. The kernel is a linear subspace of the
finite-dimensional space $V$, so it is finite-dimensional by
[[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]] and
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]]. The image is finite-dimensional because
[[lem-kernel-basis-extension-gives-image-basis]] constructs a finite basis of
it from a basis of $V$. Thus rank and nullity are natural numbers, including
when $V$ is the zero space.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis

Both dimensions are defined. The kernel is a linear subspace of the
finite-dimensional space $V$, so it is finite-dimensional by
[[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]] and
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]]. The image is finite-dimensional because

If square matrices $A$ and $B$ over $F$ are similar, then
$\operatorname{tr}(A)=\operatorname{tr}(B)$.

before.claim: If $A,B$ are Hermitian, then $\overline{\operatorname{tr}(AB)}=\operatorname{tr}((AB)^*)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ by cyclicity of trace. Hence $\operatorname{tr}(hP)$ and $\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))$ are real; $E_{xc}$ is real by [F3]. The first two terms are polynomial in the real coordinates of $P$, so together with the $C^2$ term they give a real $C^2$ function.

For real $t$, real-linearity gives $G(P+tH)=G(P)+tG(H)$. Expanding and collecting the coefficient of $t$ yields $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}((P+tH)G(P+tH))=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(H G(P)) +\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(H))$. The linear trace term differentiates to $\operatorname{tr}(hH)$ by [F1], and the $E_{xc}$ term differentiates to $\langle\nabla E_{xc}(P),H\rangle_F$ by its gradient definition.

Self-adjointness of $G$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(P G(H))=\langle P,G(H)\rangle_F=\langle G(P),H\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(G(P)H)$. Since these traces are real, the two quadratic contributions in step 1.2 combine to $\operatorname{tr}(G(P)H)$. Adding the other derivatives gives $DE(P)[H]=\langle h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P),H\rangle_F$. This is the unique Frobenius gradient pairing, so it equals $\langle F(P),H\rangle_F$.

after.claim: If $A,B$ are Hermitian, then $\overline{\operatorname{tr}(AB)}=\operatorname{tr}((AB)^*)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ by the trace identity [F4]. Hence $\operatorname{tr}(hP)$ and $\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))$ are real; $E_{xc}$ is real by [F3]. The first two terms are polynomial in the real coordinates of $P$, so together with the $C^2$ term they give a real $C^2$ function.

For real $t$, real-linearity gives $G(P+tH)=G(P)+tG(H)$. Expanding and collecting the coefficient of $t$ yields $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}((P+tH)G(P+tH))=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(H G(P)) +\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(H))$. The linear trace term differentiates to $\operatorname{tr}(hH)$ by [F1], and the $E_{xc}$ term differentiates to $\langle\nabla E_{xc}(P),H\rangle_F$ by its gradient definition.

Self-adjointness of $G$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(P G(H))=\langle P,G(H)\rangle_F=\langle G(P),H\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(G(P)H)$. Since these traces are real, the two quadratic contributions in step 1.2 combine to $\operatorname{tr}(G(P)H)$. Adding the other derivatives gives $DE(P)[H]=\langle h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P),H\rangle_F$. This is the unique Frobenius gradient pairing, so it equals $\langle F(P),H\rangle_F$.

before.quote:
For square matrices,

$$D(\operatorname{tr})(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(H).$$

For a fixed matrix $B$, the real-valued Frobenius-linear functional

$$\Phi_B(A):=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(B^\ast A)$$

satisfies

$$D\Phi_B(A)[H]=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(B^\ast H).$$

Thus the Frobenius gradient of $\Phi_B$ is $B$.

Let $S=S^*\succ0$ be an $n\times n$ finite-basis overlap matrix and supply its
Cholesky factor $L$ with $S=LL^*$, $L$ invertible
([[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]],
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]).
If $h_0=h_0^*$ is the coefficient-basis one-body matrix, set
$h=L^{-1}h_0L^{-*}$, where $L^{-*}=(L^*)^{-1}$; this is the Cholesky
whitening whose generalized Ritz quotient is preserved by
[[prop-positive-definite-overlap-whitening-preserves-generalized-ritz-pencil]].
For coefficient vectors use $y=L^*c$; the interaction map and chosen
exchange-correlation functional below are supplied in these orthonormal
coordinates. Fix $1\le r<n$ and the
projector domain $\mathcal P_r$ of [[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]].

Supply a Hermitian matrix $h$, a real-linear self-adjoint map
$G:\mathbb H_n\to\mathbb H_n$ for the Frobenius inner product, and a real-valued
$C^2$ functional $E_{xc}$ on an open neighborhood of $\mathcal P_r$. Define
$$E(P):=\operatorname{tr}(hP)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))+E_{xc}(P),\qquad F(P):=h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P).$$
Here $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius-gradient formula justified by
[[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]].

The finite-basis Hartree–Fock model is the special case $E_{xc}=0$ with a
supplied symmetry-compatible Coulomb/exchange tensor defining $G$. A
Kohn–Sham-like model supplies its density map and chosen differentiable
exchange-correlation functional. These are finite-dimensional mathematical
models; this definition makes no assertion that the selected functional is an
exact continuum physical energy.

operations.before:
Input: a complete invariant set $K$ and a gapped response map $\Phi:K\to K$
with a certified contraction factor $q<1$; an initial projector $P_0\in K$;
a certified initial error bound $E_0\ge\|P_0-P_*\|_F$ for the unique fixed
point $P_*$; residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$; finite update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$; memory $m\ge1$; coefficient cap $C\ge1$; and an eigensolver
which, on success at $X$, returns $\widetilde\Phi(X)\in K$ and a certified
$\eta(X)\ge0$ with $\|\widetilde\Phi(X)-\Phi(X)\|_F\le\eta(X)$. The solver
returns a separate failure status if it cannot certify the gap or this error.

For $k=0,\ldots,N$:

1. If no certified response evaluation is cached for $P_k$, evaluate the finite-basis matrix $F(P_k)$ and its occupied projector solver. If the gap fails, return $\texttt{gap-loss}$; if the eigensolver cannot certify its output/error, return $\texttt{eigensolve-failure}$. Retain the evaluated pair $(P_k,F(P_k))$ for this proposal step and set $\bar\rho_k=\|P_k-\widetilde\Phi(P_k)\|_F+\eta(P_k)$. If $\bar\rho_k\le\varepsilon$, return $\texttt{residual-tolerance-met}$ with error bound $\bar\rho_k/(1-q)$.
2. If $k=N$, return $\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted}$ with current bound $E_k$.
3. Call [[alg-capped-diis-projector-proposal]] with the up-to-$m-1$ preceding stored pairs and the current pair $(P_k,F(P_k))$. For a candidate $Y$, certify $Y\in K$, the gap at $Y$, and one eigensolver evaluation $\widetilde\Phi(Y)$ with error $\eta(Y)$. Accept $Y$ only if all certificates succeed and
$$\frac{\|Y-\widetilde\Phi(Y)\|_F+\eta(Y)}{1-q}\le qE_k.$$
If accepted, set $P_{k+1}=Y$ and $E_{k+1}=qE_k$.
4. If the DIIS system is singular/uncertified, its candidate gap fails, or its fixed-point residual test fails, use the baseline update from step 1: set $P_{k+1}=\widetilde\Phi(P_k)$ and $E_{k+1}=qE_k+\eta(P_k)$. If the baseline certificate or $K$-membership check fails, return its distinct gap, eigensolver, or invariance-certificate failure status.
5. Append the current pair $(P_k,F(P_k))$ to the preceding-iterate history, retaining at most the newest $m-1$ preceding pairs. If step 3 accepted $Y$, cache its certified evaluation $(F(Y),\widetilde\Phi(Y),\eta(Y))$ as the next iteration's current evaluation; if the baseline branch was used, evaluate its new iterate when the next loop begins. Never attach a response matrix evaluated at one density to a different density.

The DIIS commutator objective is only a proposal score. Acceptance uses the
separate fixed-point residual $\|Y-\Phi(Y)\|_F$ with its additive eigensolver
error certificate. The algorithm makes no unconditional success claim: finite
budget exhaustion and each certificate failure are explicit outcomes.

operations.before: Statement: Steps 2.1–2.2 cover nonunique least-squares minimizers, including a singular Gram matrix, and prove a unique minimum-norm tie-break.
operations.after: The singular-Gram/nonunique least-squares case retains existence and the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm selection. Current Proof3.1: For $c,d\in\mathcal C_{s,C}$ and $0\le t\le1$, the coefficients $e=(1-t)c+td$ satisfy $\sum_i e_i=(1-t)\sum_i c_i+t\sum_i d_i=1$. By [F3], $\sum_i|e_i|\le(1-t)\sum_i|c_i|+t\sum_i|d_i|\le C$, so $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ is convex. The set $M$ is also convex: for matrices $A,B$ the identity $\|(1-t)A+tB\|_F^2=(1-t)\|A\|_F^2+t\|B\|_F^2-t(1-t)\|A-B\|_F^2$ proves convexity of the squared norm. Applying it to $A=\sum_i c_iR_i$ and $B=\sum_i d_iR_i$ shows $J((1-t)c+td)\le(1-t)J(c)+tJ(d)=\min J$, so the convex combination also minimizes. Since $M$ is compact, the continuous function $c\mapsto\|c\|_2^2$ has a minimizer $c_*\in M$. Current Proof4.1: If distinct $c,d\in M$ both had minimum Euclidean norm, their midpoint would lie in $M$ and satisfy $\left\|\frac{c+d}{2}\right\|_2^2=\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2}-\frac{\|c-d\|_2^2}{4}<\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2},$ contradicting minimality. Thus $c_*$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares minimizer. No nonsingularity of the Gram matrix is needed for existence or tie-breaking.
